one_liner: Header-only learned index over sorted integer arrays that matches B+-tree lookup latency with an index orders of magnitude smaller.
what_it_does: Builds a small index over a sorted array of numeric keys that you keep and own. pgm::PGMIndex::search(key) returns an approximate position plus a window [lo, hi) of at most about 2*Epsilon+2 slots, and you finish the lookup with std::lower_bound over that window, so it is not a container and not a drop-in for std::map or a B+-tree. Other classes cover related cases: DynamicPGMIndex is a map-like container with insert_or_assign, erase, find, lower_bound, range and forward iterators, and there are compressed, Elias-Fano, bucketing, mmap-backed (MappedPGMIndex) and multidimensional variants. It also ships a C interface for int32/int64/uint32/uint64 keys and a Python wrapper (PyGM).
how_it_is_fast: It computes an optimal piecewise linear epsilon-approximation (a convex-hull streaming algorithm) of the key-to-rank function, so each segment of (first key, float slope, uint32 intercept) predicts a position within +/-Epsilon. It then indexes the segment keys recursively with the same method (EpsilonRecursive defaults to 4), which gives a short tree with a linear scan over a few segments at each level instead of storing every key in inner nodes the way a B+-tree does. Because the index has m segments with m often 2-5 orders of magnitude below n, it stays in cache, and construction is one linear pass per level, parallelised with OpenMP when available.
when_to_use: Read-mostly sorted arrays of 32/64-bit integer (or float/double) keys that need point, predecessor/lower_bound or range queries at B+-tree-like latency, with the index taking KiB-MiB instead of hundreds of MiB (paper: 87 KiB vs 874 MiB on 715M keys).
Keys with a smooth or locally linear distribution, such as timestamps, log offsets or mostly sequential IDs, where few segments are needed and the index fits in L2/L3.
Memory-constrained services or large mmap'd sorted key files (MappedPGMIndex), where a per-key index structure would not fit in RAM.
You need a guaranteed worst-case search window (a fixed epsilon bound) rather than the data-dependent error of an RMI.
Write-heavy integer key/value workloads on a single thread, where DynamicPGMIndex's LSM-style merging gave the highest insert throughput in the independent GRE benchmark at 100% writes.
when_not_to_use: Point-lookup latency matters more than memory: in the independent SOSD benchmark (200M 32-bit amzn keys) PGM took 326 ns, against 181 ns for RMI, 267 ns for RadixSpline and about 94-115 ns for hash tables that use far more memory.

Read-heavy dynamic workloads: in the authors' own paper the Dynamic PGM was 1.0% and 15.2% slower than the best B+-tree at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions, and GRE found its lookups dominated by ALEX and LIPP.
String, composite or wider-than-word keys: the author says it is made for integers that fit in a machine word (issue #8), and key differences are converted to double for prediction.
Builds with MSVC (the __int128 use breaks it, issue #19 still open), with -fno-exceptions (issue #56 open), or with concurrent writers (DynamicPGMIndex has no synchronisation).
Hard-to-learn distributions, such as SOSD's Hilbert-projected osm cell IDs, where learned indexes lost to a simple radix lookup table and gave little gain over binary search.

integration.dependencies: None required. OpenMP is optional and parallelises construction (without it you get a '#pragma message' warning). A BSD-licensed SDSL subset (sdsl.hpp) is bundled for the compressed and Elias-Fano variants. MultidimensionalPGMIndex needs BMI2/AVX2, and MappedPGMIndex uses POSIX mmap.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17; README uses g++ -std=c++17); GCC or Clang, because it uses __int128, __builtin_clzll and __builtin_prefetch. CI builds gcc and clang on ubuntu-22.04 and macos-12, with a gcc 13.2 fix in 2024. MSVC is not supported.
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS on x86-64 and arm64 (an Apple arm64 compile issue was fixed in 2021). On Windows only MinGW-w64 is reported to work. The multidimensional variant is x86-only (BMI2 _pdep/_pext). The bundled CMake adds -march=native.
integration.thread_safety: The author says in issue #16 that all classes except DynamicPGMIndex are read-only after construction and safe for concurrent reads without synchronisation. DynamicPGMIndex has no internal locking, and concurrent use is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — PGMIndex replaces only the search structure over a sorted array you already keep, not the B+-tree container itself. DynamicPGMIndex is a map-like container, but its API differs from STX btree_map/std::map: no operator[], size() is O(n), and iterators are forward-only.

gotchas: Sentinel values: std::numeric_limits<K>::max() (or infinity for floating-point keys) is reserved. Building on data that contains it throws, and querying it in DynamicPGMIndex segfaulted (issue #36); the GRE benchmark had to shift Facebook keys by -1. In DynamicPGMIndex with an arithmetic value type, numeric_limits<V>::max() is the delete tombstone and cannot be stored.

Floating-point precision: slopes default to float (the paper used double). Users saw keys fall outside the returned [lo, hi) window on the SOSD books and GRE eth datasets (issues #30 and #45), and the author's fix was Floating=double or a wider search window. Results can differ across CPUs and compilers.
Segment intercepts are uint32_t, so indexing more than about 4.29 billion positions throws overflow_error('Change the type of Segment::intercept to uint64'), which means editing the header.

Errors are reported by throwing exceptions (unsorted input, the sentinel value, the tombstone value). DynamicPGMIndex::lower_bound tracks tombstoned keys in a std::set while scanning levels, so delete-heavy data slows it. An untriaged 2025 comment on issue #63 reports a wrong lookup for a duplicate-heavy uint64 array built on 2 cores.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PGM over CARMI when index footprint and a provable epsilon-bounded search window matter more than raw lookup speed: CARMI claims an average 2.2x over the STX B+Tree but still uses about 0.77x the B+Tree's memory, while PGM's index is KiB-MiB. Pick rafaelkallis ART instead for a general mutable ordered map with byte-string keys; libmdbx, redb and TerarkDB are persistent transactional stores, not in-memory search indexes, so they do not substitute.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' own PVLDB'20 experiments (2.3 GHz Xeon Gold with no model stated, compiler and flags not given, no stdlib baseline), on 715M 8-byte Web-log keys with 128-byte payloads and 10M random queries, PGM matched the fastest STX B+-tree v0.9 latency with an 87 KiB index against 874 MiB and matched the fastest CSS-tree with 4 MiB against 341 MiB. The Dynamic PGM (epsilon 64, 1B keys, 10M mixed operations) was 13-71% faster than the STX B+-tree except at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions. The independent SOSD benchmark (Xeon Gold 6230) confirms PGM beats a B-tree (326 vs 482 ns, 14 vs 166 MB) but contradicts the paper's claim that it dominates RMI, blaming the paper's weaker RMI implementation.
status_note: Stale: the last commit was 2024-11-28 (edge-case fixes for float and one-element inputs), and 12 issues are open, including MSVC and noexcept requests. It is Apache-2.0 and header-only, and the core static index is two headers of about 630 lines, so it is easy to vendor.
